speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: asked the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health regarding the Singapore Medical Foundation AI Model (SIMFONI) initiative (a) what are the rationale and cost of developing AI models for conditions that can be diagnosed by routine tests, instead of targeting rare diseases that are harder to diagnose; (b) how will clinicians access SIMFONI and whether private practitioners will be included; and (c) what safeguards protect patient identifiers from data leaks.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: asked the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (a) before the deployment of Singapore Medical Foundation AI Model (SIMFONI), whether the Ministry will subject its models to privacy testing by assessors independent of the developers to determine if they can memorise or reproduce identifiable patient information; and (b) whether test standards, findings and response protocol for any disclosure will be published.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are starting with a couple of specialty areas and settings in the public healthcare sector.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If successful, we will expand its coverage to more specialities and also possibly, to the private practitioners.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This platform is called TRUST, which was established in 2022 precisely for research, development and innovation efforts.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While clinicians will ultimately retain responsibility for medical decisions, international experience has shown that doctors may gradually defer to AI decisions or recommendations – something known as automation bias.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the Ministry announce specific safeguards to detect and mitigate this risk and how we ensure that AI compliments rather than subtly replaces independent clinical judgement?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We do not really announce what we are going to do to safeguard against this.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is very much in the way we approach AI, how we deploy and how we implement them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I have given a few speeches on this matter.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is a lot of hype about AI, including in healthcare.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And sometimes, you really wonder why are these proposals like that.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That means, what problems are we facing, can AI solve those problems?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Never treat AI as a hammer going around looking for nails or a solution looking for a problem.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Let us see what AI can do to solve some of these problems.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And when you can find the right AI tool, make sure it is trained in the local context, taking into account security, de-identified data, patient data that is in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When the model is ready, when you deploy it, you have to deploy in accordance with clinical protocols.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is a certain way we do things.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: AI is not something you plug into the socket and suddenly, it solves your problems.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And then, how do you interface with existing legacy IT systems?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: How the processes are thought through, with the clinicians still making the judgement?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is early days, but I think we are very conscious that there is a lot of hype, a lot of use or misuse of AI.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think all this hype at some point will subside to a more realistic level, where people are more judicious, thoughtful and even, sober about using AI.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And we tell ourselves, "Why wait for that process?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Why do we not start off being sober and judicious?" And that is the approach that the Ministry of Health is taking.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would it encompass all health data in Singapore of all patients, including data in the National Electronic Health Record (NEHR) database?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Has the Ministry considered, or will the Ministry consider, asking patients for explicit consent before their data can be used for training purposes?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And third supplementary question: I understand the Minister has given assurances that the data will be anonymised and have personal identifiers removed before they are used for training.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, as we can see, I have another Parliamentary Question today for a similar data leak incident with the Singapore Land Authority, where a lot of these processes are fallible.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And sometimes, anonymisation of data does not actually pan out and personal identifiable data can leak into publicly available databases.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What assurances can the Minister give to the public that their very sensitive health data will remain safe?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think we all know AI is a breakthrough technology, but we must take a thoughtful and judicious approach.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, we have to decide what we want to do with it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Make sure that it is anonymised and de-identified.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think we make sure it is anonymised and de-identified by international standards.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And at some point, Singaporeans will see that healthcare services are improving, yet quite incident-free.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That is when they have confidence and assurance.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think let the action and the results speak for themselves.
